text:
A lot of people seem to forget that VRAM is important, but it is NOT the most important thing. Typically 12GB of VRAM is enough for most games on 1440p, but 16GB future proofs practically all games at the 1440p setting (Don't really think 4k is all that different from 1440p in quality and i've played with both). 

Once you find that 16GB VRAM sweet spot, you want to focus on the Clock Speed, whether it can be overclocked, how many bits and shading units, the quality of the build (make sure those drivers don't fail) and so much more. 

A GPU is not just defined by the amount of VRAM, it has.

text: Price is actually very important & translates to "You get what you pay for".  Granted, Nvidia prices are quite high - especially when it comes to the 40 Series cards.  20 Series cards were extremely high when they launched.  However, the quality is unmatched.  I've used both Nvidia & AMD cards in the past.  In the end, Nvidia was the better choice.  It's the same principle with regards to AMD vs Intel CPUs.  Again, I've had both AMD & Intel CPU systems.  Intel was the better CPU in the end.  As previously stated - you get what you pay for folks.  Some may disagree with me but I'm just going off my personal experience.  As for Intel's GPUs, I would steer clear of these until all the issues are worked out.  Since Intel is a newcomer into the GPU market, there are bound to be issues with an introductory product as is clearly the case here.  For the record, I am all for competition in the marketplace.  Over the past 20+ years there have been countless corporate buyouts/mergers which have stifled innovation/competition in the marketplace which in turn has lead to overly-inflated prices for generally inferior quality products/services.  Case in point - Dell's acquisition of the Alienware brand back in '06.  Prior to the Dell buyout/merger, Alienware was one of the very best makers of high-end gaming desktop/laptop PCs.  Not anymore.  Dell has run Alienware into the ground.  Gamers Nexus' videos regarding the $5K Alienware R13 prove just how far Alienware has fallen from its glory days pre-Dell buyout/merger.  Prebuilt PCs are bound to be trouble/have issues & have tons of crapware preinstalled on them anyway.  Regardless, when it comes to CPUs/GPUs, you get what you pay for.  The initial Intel GPU offerings prove this.  It's obvious Intel's ARC GPUs are in a beta stage & as such, are likely to have issues as is clearly the case according to what's shown in the video provided by Gamers Nexus here.  Hopefully Intel can work out the kinks & provide some much-needed competition in the GPU space.

text:
This is a virtually unsellable product. I literally can't think of anyone with any use case who would seriously consider buying one of these.

If you are the type of tech-savvy power-user/tinkerer who is used to troubleshooting and being an early-adopter of cutting edge tech, you're almost certainly going to want a more powerful offering anyway. Casual PC gamer? You're gonna go with a tried-and-true reliable Nvidia card that's essentially plug-and-play. PC gaming is already intimidating to more casual gamers who would be better off spending a bit more in exchange for a reliable Nvidia GPU that just works.

What is the target market for this product? Who would seriously pay to beta test this thing for Intel??

"It's a decent first showing! Not bad! I'm excited to see where this goes!" -> yeah, no. The reality is that nobody is going to shell out $300 for a GPU that can't play every game; that's way too much money! When someone spends that kinda cash on a graphics card, they expect it to play all their games. If it was $100, fine, but at $300 there's just no market for this product.

I can't fathom a single person seriously considering this card as the one GPU they run in their one computer. Everyone is going to choose to spend slightly more for a 3060 or get slightly worse performance with a 3050 in exchange for having a card that isn't a science project.

This ignores the reality that AMD exists and makes excellent cards (though as a content creator I'm admittedly stuck with Nvidia cuz of NVENC), as well as the fact that Intel's GPUs are launching now yet comparing themselves to what will be Nvidia's prior generation.

I agree; it's a solid first showing and I'm hopeful that Intel keeps going with it and competes with AMD and Nvidia, but I ain't buying it, and neither are any of you! Intel said they'd price the card based on Tier 3 performance, but they didn't. I don't know how Intel moves forward with this project when literally nobody but SIs will buy this card.

Steve is right - consistency is king. I'd rather a video take an extra minute to encode but never fail than have it go slightly faster but fail even 1% of the time. Instantaneous benchmarks aren't the end-all.

tl;dr - Seeing all these comments from people who are never going to buy this card that say: "hey! It's pretty good for a first attempt" just really annoyed me, especially as an Intel shareholder. Sure, it's a solid attempt and a promising sign for the future, but it's still not a card that any segment of the market would actually buy. These cards will not sell, and thus the product is inadequate.

If it was really a great value card, people would buy them. I'm almost certain nobody will.

text:
Despite GN doing everything they can to dissuade people from getting this card I think gave enough information to convince some people to consider this card.

The performance scaling at higher resolutions is a big selling point.

The DX11 and earlier performance is abysmal but once you go past DX11 we are talking about very old games. Even though the performance is bad for the price the performance level is going to be playable in terms of average FPS. The real major concern is the frame pacing. It has been reported the stuttering can be garbage and if that occurs in too many games that's a much more important issue than losing half to 70% of your expected average FPS because it makes the games uncomfortable to play or down right unplayable.


This review doesn't cover Xess vs DLSS/FSR or raytracing technologies but it is clear Intel is almost on par with Nvidia with these 2 technologies which gives another valid reason to choose Intel over AMD.

If you want to play 4K cheaply then Intel actually looks god. You simply have to make sure your games aren't buggy with their cards (not being to launch fortnite of all games is inexcusable and a clear sign you need to find out how much of your game library isn't supported)

If you want to play at 1080p cheaply then AMD is definitely the route you should be going.

If you want to play at 1440p cheaply you have to lean AMD for now, because while Intel has clear advantages when it works the headaches don't seem worth gambling on for that level of performance at that resolution.

My gut instinct from the way it's scaling with resolution and where it's struggling or outright breaking is that somthing in the drivers is inducing a slowdown, (probably a per frame delay of a few processing cycles), that becomes more and more relevant the higher the framerate goes. High resolutions and demanding games, (and their lower average framerates), would minimise this and let the GPU stretch more. 

Obvious test would be to take something it does ok in like TWW3 and lower the graphics settings for a retest at the same resolution and see if raising the average framerates that way messes with the results in the same way as messing with the resolution.

text:
Intel have driver issues with the A770 leading to no display signal and impacted performance when reviewing leading up to release: GN talks about driver issues and that it can impact usability of the card.

AMD have driver issues with the 5000 series leading to software clock/tuning settings not setting right when reviewing leading up to release: GN talks about driver issues and it can impact usability of the card.

Nvidia have driver issues with the 3000 series leading to no display signal and impacted performance when reviewing leading up to release: GN acknowledge the driver issues and note that results and conclusions are pending Nvidia fixing their drivers and sending them their way.



Weird to point this out given that GN is typically a solid unbiased group that hold companies to their shii, but just because a company like Nvidia is big, loud and likes to throw their weight around shouldn't impact reactions to situations when it occurs to them where two companies get points deducted and included as part of the review, whilst another gets a "we'll hold off and let you fix it and factor it out of the review".

Previous it was possible to put it down to Steves obvious frustration and annoyance at AMD over certain things, but when Intel get the same treatment as AMD then suddenly it looks more like Nvidia is the one getting singled out for differing treatment.

Perhaps I have become so accustomed to the GN reviews being calm, objective events, that when confronted by anger at the beginning of a review, and seemingly, uncalled attacks throughout, it stopped seeming like a review and became to be an op-ed. text:
I kind of feel like they should’ve just eaten the cost on these things to such an extent that they were practically or actually giving them away as part of a wider scale testing process.

They could have simply loaned a couple thousand of these to people who really wanted to participate in a relatively open beta.  Ideally some folks that have a lot of free time to log some serious hours gaming on them.  It would cost them shipping, and probably a few cards that got wrecked or kept, but I’m sure there would have been people who either couldn’t get GPUs six months ago or would have just wanted something fun to play with, and then just make it mandatory for anyone in the program to consent to some extensive telemetry data collection during the testing period, including video clips and screenshots so they can see exactly what happened.  That’s the only way I think they could’ve caught up a little bit on their software.

I thought it was really interesting when they went on tour making videos with creators explaining what they were doing differently and showing off all of the unique things about their technology, and I really think they could develop these into something really cool someday—but that requires lots of users and lots of time to do, and their only options are to slowly bleed out in the market, hoping that someone will buy it at a price greater than zero OR do something like I suggested. Either way they’re all gonna lose money on these fucking things, but with my method of Front loading all of that loss, by temporarily loaning the hardware to people, there’s a chance they can get a bunch of those back in Salem on the used market once the software is good, they could sell them to the users at a discount, but at least they won’t sell someone an over priced piece of shit that needs a little more time to get right.

I have a feeling however, that much of their issues with wildly inconsistent performance has everything to do with the fact that they built these damn things to run with rebar and in their optimal configuration. When AMD launched their smart access memory (a.k.a. resizable bar) testing showed wildly inconsistent results Where it made a huge difference in some titles, where it made no difference, and most importantly where it made a negative difference in performance. They really need to figure out how to get their cards to run reasonably well without rebar, and they have to figure out which games are benefiting from it and which games are not, so that when rebar is enabled it won’t actually run in that mode when it’s actually harmful to the performance in certain games.  I know that was something AMD had to do, but it seems like they worked that out.

text:
I don't know why, but this review just doesn't sit well with me.  I have no problem with the data or the critique of the product, but Steve just seems so negative about this launch.  It's not perfect, but it is far from trash and we should all be excited about a third party entering the market with such a good first showing.  The fact that it's trading blows 1:1 in so many areas this early in the product cycle of a first gen release is nothing short of amazing and a credit to the work Intel engineers put into this product.  

I noticed this with the last few product cycles, and with the LTT warranty issue, Steve just does not seem happy or excited about technology anymore.  It seems like GN has taken the "journalistic integrity" to such an extreme that it is isolating them from the community of reviewers, journalists, and consumers.  I watched Paul, Jay, and Linus's take on the ARC and all of them voices the same concerns and criticizes as Steve did, but they were also so happy to be working with this product, to see everything that has gone into this new product and they encouraged people who are willing to help make it better to buy it, to not be afraid of it, and to become part of the market disruption we all keep claiming we want but still go buy from big green because "more fps".  I will keep watching GN for their excellent data and testing, but I have to admit that I need to watch other people first because GN treats everyone as an enemy of the people and it's just getting a bit depressing.

text:
I would normally agree with Steve with pretty much anything but I think he's perhaps being too negative.

First off, this card isn't going to be for most of us. If we're watching GN, we're more likely to be owning or aiming to buy much more capable hardware. The thing is, we're not the target consumer for Arc A7 anyway.

Nvidia and AMD have become absolutely shambolic with their price/performance offerings at the lower end of the market. Doesn't affect us? Well it does. PC gaming has reached an amazing state with unprecedented amounts of console ports, Japanese games and indie offerings. This is because the entry into PC gaming was superb value for money, even when compared to consoles. The industry now puts PC gaming on an equal priority to the consoles, no longer an afterthought.

Now if Nvidia and AMD are no longer giving budget/mainstream gamers an upgrade option with an attractive price/performance ratio, they won't be able to play the latest PC games and will most likely go back to console gaming. Devs will be less likely to port their console games and the PC gaming industry will start to decline.

It seems like the silicon in the A7 is capable, what's needed is driver maturity and that will happen in time. Hopefully Intel can leverage their huge presence in the OEM market to get these cards "sold".

Remember if Arc is a success, we will all benefit from it.

text:
All the bad stuff aside, i am still generally excited by this.  Why?  Because driver issues can be resolved.  Once these drivers issues are resolved, it means we have a legitimate third player on the market which can only be good for the consumer.

While i agree with Gamers Nexus that i certainly wouldn't recommend it to a non enthusiast, and to an enthusiast who is looking for something that just works it's also not a great choice, i really do think in 3-6 months we could be seeing a very different picture and a very different GPU landscape, and that some sanity might come back to this world where gamers can actually find cards that play the games they like at reasonable framerates under $400.

Since i'm also a car guy i'll use this analogy, this card feels like you have a really nice Cosworth engine strapped to a crappy inefficient transmission that slips gears, etc.  If they can sort out the transmission issues and get that power efficiently and consistently to the ground, i think they'll have a slam dunk value/perf card here, the space that x60 and x70 cars used to operate in 10xx series and prior with Nvidia, and to some extent AMD still operates in.

Side note, I do think the card looks great.  I love the subdued understated look, i love that it's not 2.7+ slots and just a gigantic brick in your system like most other cards these days.  The lighting strip on it looks classy, etc.  I think Intel scored a big win in this department.

text:
To be honest, this is about what I expected from this launch. Intel isn't new to graphics processors, obviously, but they are new to the discrete GPU game. When you are jumping into that world as a newcomer with no former development of previous discrete cards to evolve from (outside of the Xe DG1), there are going to be glaring issues and hiccups no matter how prepared you wanted to be. I remember when these cards were announced, my first thought was that they look promising, but were going to need quite a bit of time to iron out all the issues that are going to crop up right out of the gate. These cards will need at the very least 6-12 months of being in customers hands to figure out the real world issues and start optimizing them. Even then, we won't see the potential of what these cards can do until a second iteration comes out. So none of these results or complaints are in the least bit surprising to me. Shouldn't have been to anyone else, either. But, I have a feeling that a year or so down the road, when Intel has had the time to really thoroughly comb through these cards with the real world data coming back from customers, they will be in a solid place for their price point. Just to be clear, I by no means am defending Intel or giving them a pass simply because they are new to the discrete GPU game, but let's be real here... You have to start somewhere! And early adopters were always going to be "beta testers" for these cards. They are going to need time to evolve their architecture and mature in this space, just like AMD & Nvidia had to when they jumped in. Still, pretty ruff start when a week out from launch, the most basic drivers aren't working properly.

With all that said, I just hope they iron out the wrinkles quickly. We need more competition in the discrete GPU space. Afterall, these cards are going to form the foundation for the future of Intel cards, if they have a long term future in this space. But hey, they are in the "ballpark" at least! Already competing with much more established brands/cards of similar spec, even with the issues. So that is good! They just have a long way to go with the consistency from game to game. So I still find them promising. Just going to take awhile to get them where they need to be with optimization & drivers for broad appeal.

text:
I think we can blame a certain amount of this on Microsoft for their DirectX 9 to DirectX 12 translation layer. And before anyone says that this is a silly idea in general, remember the Valve Steamdeck exists. 

I say this because they use "proton" to translate Direct X calls to Vulcan. They're even sometimes capable of running native windows apps that use DirectX on the Linux better than they run on PC. (But those are special cases).

Still, it's incredibly annoying that Microsoft doesn't have a decent translation layer built into their drivers.

The silly thing is, Proton is open source. I wonder if there's a viable path to port Proton to windows so Intel can use it in their drivers.

@OnTheRocks71  I saw on videos form tech-channels that do "unofficial repairing of broken GPUs" (they have lots of instruments/tools hardware testers etc for this task)
(they are getting parts from China, you can order any part of Nvidia GPU from small elements to memory/chip main elements)
they can easily repair any Nvidia 30XX for cost less than new gpu, obviously. 

And reason for Nvidia GPU getting broken is very obviously - something burn on board or some physical damage or water. They had no cases with Nvidia GPU that "something magic happened inside of chip and whole GPU become brick".

And they show also "alot" of broken AMD-6000 GPUs with identical symptoms - 1 year of use and just died randomly for no reason (GPUs came from many users, for about 6 months). They showed that every (100+ just on video) GPU has same case - short circuit inside of chip (they showed it on electric sensor and thermal) in same place of chip for every GPU.

And reason why not a single of those GPU can be fixed - because AMD put memory chips inside "main chip". To replace main chip - you basically need to replace chip+memory that is 99% of GPU cost - obviously cost same or more than new AMD GPU.

And their conclusion was - this all could happen only because defect in chip, it can be "error in chip scheme" or manufacturer of AMD gpu chips sabotaging quality of chips and shipping them in this "low quality broken state" (and AMD dont care for some reason).

If there were an issue causing games to crash or not work with D3D9on12, it'd probably get fixed since using it on Windows is its primary use case, whereas DXVK Windows support is mostly provided as-is and they won't try to fix Windows-only issues. text:
Eh.. I get the head to head with Nvidia and not including AMD. Despite AMD's social media advantage - most of the online community will root AMD  - when it comes to actual consumers and buyers, AMD cards are at a massive disadvantage. They are never in short supply despite being produced in much smaller numbers - because people really don't use them. This can be proved with a variety of metrics, be it supply vs demand, or looking at a few thousand setups online and playing count the AMD cards (typically you only see them in all AMD builds), etc, pick whatever you want it comes out the same. AMD isn't a real competitor... yet.

I'm not saying they aren't good cards, just that they aren't really wanted. It's like RC vs Coke/Pepsi. I have no doubt eventually AMD will surpass Nvidia in actual performance/quality - I leave out price because the differences really aren't that big if you're going to use the GPU for multiple years. IE: A $50 or even a $100 difference over 3 years is negligible - but even then it'll be multiple generations after that before they'll actually be able to compete head to head. Years of beating them on performance, because that's what it takes to really win a brand fight. Brand recognition and the power that comes with it is a big deal that doesn't really care about things like "Well this actually a better performance for dollar." If it was that simple, well there wouldn't be so many monopolies out there across all the industries, because there is always a better performance to dollar competitor, it just doesn't really matter at scale.
